video:video.video:title: AML Watcher Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The recurring price is only visible after you set the search volume in the calculator, so we cannot give a monthly number. There is a one-time set-up cost on Basic and Premium, unused credits do not roll over, extra searches are billed at the end of the cycle, and cancelling means emailing sales.

video:video.video:title: Alohi Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catch is that Alohi is a suite of separate products: Fax.Plus, Sign.Plus, Scan.Plus: each with its own subscription, so "one ecosystem" can mean several line items if you want e-signatures and faxing and scanning. Page and member limits on the lower tiers are modest, and HIPAA/BAA sits only on the top tier. For a single job (say online faxing), it's clean and cheap; for the full workflow, add up the parts.

video:video.video:title: Atto Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Simple and honest pricing: the real conversation with any field-team tracker is the human one: GPS tracking of employees needs transparency and often consent (rules differ by country), and adoption dies the day the crew feels surveilled rather than served. Roll it out as 'accurate paychecks and fewer timesheet fights', involve the team, and the tool pays for itself; roll it out as surveillance and no feature list saves it.

video:video.video:title: BackupMaster Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The listing header says free to install, and there is a free tier, but it is not for you unless you are an agency: Agency is limited to Shopify Partner development stores before they are handed over to a client. For a live store the entry price is $19 a month and it buys 300 orders a month.
Restore is described on the listing as restoring supported items, and the list of what that excludes lives in the documentation rather than on the listing. It matters. Read on 10 October 2026, the coverage page says orders are backed up but cannot be restored or cloned, because Shopify limits updates to existing orders. Locations, saved searches, policies and shipping zones are backup-only, and inventory comes back only through a manual download and Shopify's own inventory import. Store settings, third-party app data, reviews, redirects, coupons, companies, catalogs and analytics are not covered at all. Read that page before you rely on the product, and run one real restore into a development store rather than discovering the boundary during an incident.
The most useful review on the page is the critical one. In April 2026 a merchant asked for exports over SFTP to storage the vendor does not control, on-demand backups before risky changes, configurable retention and languages beyond English and German. The same merchant noted that a second store costs extra here where some rivals include one. None of that is damning; it is a fair map of where this app currently stops. One of those requests has since been met in part: the documentation now describes a Backup Now button for a manual backup at any time (read 10 October 2026). Worth adding to the same note: your store data sits with a vendor in Australia, which belongs in your processing register whatever you decide.

video:video.video:title: Barcodes Talk Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest caveat is about fit, not the codes. Some large retailers and brand registries (notably certain Amazon Brand Registry and big-box requirements) increasingly ask for a GS1-issued prefix tied to your own company, and a third-party barcode (legitimate and globally unique as it is) may not satisfy that specific gatekeeping. For most marketplaces and independent retail it's completely fine and far cheaper; just confirm your channel's exact requirement first.

video:video.video:title: Beautiful.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The smart-template engine is the feature and the fence: decks look polished with zero design skill precisely because the system constrains you, so pixel-perfect custom layouts and heavy brand exceptions fight the tool. And note the billing gap: $14.50/mo annual becomes $45 month-to-month, one of the steeper monthly premiums around. If your organisation lives in PowerPoint workflows, test the import/export round-trip before committing.

video:video.video:title: BillingNow Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing is refreshing: two plans, same features on both, unlimited users, no per-seat maths. The honest watch-out is the trial length rather than its terms: three days is short for migrating billing into a new tool, and the practical constraint is that there is no import path. The help centre documents CSV and Excel export but no import, so an existing client list has to be retyped, which is more than three days of work for anyone with a real book. It is also a young product from a small Geneva maker, so weigh integration depth and longevity before you move your billing history in.

video:video.video:title: Blinq Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The core product is honestly cheap: the cost that grows sits in events, at $500 per Campaign on pay as you go, or $2,999 a year for five events, on top of the Business seats (read 24 November 2026; the leads themselves are not charged per lead), which is where teams that live on trade shows actually get value. And a truth about all digital cards: the wow factor works precisely because adoption is still low; the durable value is the CRM sync (contacts flowing automatically into your pipeline), so judge Business tier by that integration, not by the tap-to-share trick.

video:video.video:title: BookX Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free plan is a demonstration rather than a plan. One service and one team member means a salon with two stylists, or a studio running two class types, is already on Starter, so treat $4.99 a month as the real entry price, not zero. From there the ladder is gated on locations and team members rather than on how much you actually book: five, ten and twenty at $4.99, $9.99 and $19.99. A busy single-location business therefore pays the same as a quiet one, which is generous, while a small chain climbs the ladder for reasons that have nothing to do with volume. Above twenty locations or team members the published table stops and you have to ask. And the whole thing only exists inside Shopify (the calendar rides on your storefront, checkout and POS) so there is nothing here for a business that takes bookings anywhere else.

video:video.video:title: Browse.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest realities of no-code scraping. Credits burn faster than expected: row counts, screenshots and 'premium' sites all multiply the meter, so monitor a big site daily and do the math first. And scrapers break when sites redesign: robots need maintenance, which is your time even when the tool is no-code. Also check the terms of the sites you monitor; 'technically possible' and 'permitted' aren't the same thing.

video:video.video:title: Cal.com Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Team features such as round-robin, collective events, routing forms and removing the Cal.com branding need a paid plan. SMS reminders use prepaid credits and the price per text is not shown. In our test the app stayed in Dutch until we changed the language to another one and back, and the default links were created in Dutch. We did not test calendar sync.

video:video.video:title: Claude Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catch is usage limits: even on Pro you can hit a ceiling mid-session on a heavy day, and the step up to Max is a real $100 to $200 a month: you're buying headroom, not extra features. It also doesn't generate images, so if that's your main need it's the wrong tool, and it has fewer third-party plugins than ChatGPT.

video:video.video:title: Clutch Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's free to submit a brief, but be clear on what it is: a lead-generation marketplace, not a neutral directory. Your brief goes straight to agencies who will reach out to pitch you, and providers pay to be visible and matched. It's a fast way to shortlist vetted agencies; just expect the outreach that comes with it.

video:video.video:title: Contractor Foreman Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Credit where it is due first: this is company pricing with unlimited projects and no per-user overage inside your tier, which is rare in construction software and cheaper than per-seat rivals for a crew. The catch is the billing term. Monthly costs 20% to 32% more than annual on the same plan, $139 against $105 on Standard, and Basic is sold on annual billing only, so the cheapest way in requires a year paid up front. The user counts are the real ladder: 1, 3, 8, 15, unlimited. A five-person crew is not on Standard at $105, it is on Plus at $166, so count your licence holders before you compare against anything else.

video:video.video:title: Databox Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing has moved upmarket. On 12 November 2026 the page sold one self-serve plan, Business, at $399 a month billed annually ($499 monthly) for up to 10 users, 30 data sources and 1,500 AI credits a month. The free plan and the cheaper Analyst, Team Core and Team Scale tiers we read in October are gone, so a solo user or a small team now pays the same entry price as a ten-person one. Only the Agency plan sells capacity piecemeal, from $79 a month plus $20 account packs. AI credits are a shared monthly pool for Genie and the MCP server, and 15-minute sync, once part of the top plan, is now a $14 per-source add-on on top of the subscription. Power users may also find the custom-metric and data-modelling depth limited next to a full BI tool.

video:video.video:title: Deputy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The minimum monthly spend is the number to check before anything else: at $5.50 per user on monthly billing, a team of fewer than about six people still pays the $30 floor, so the headline per-user price is misleading at small scale. Beyond that, the plan you probably want is not the one you first price: auto-scheduling, demand forecasting and labour budgets sit in Core, and SSO, custom access levels and location hierarchies only in Pro, which has no public self-serve checkout. The add-ons stack per user as well, and the payroll add-on is US-only and annual-only.

video:video.video:title: Descript Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's per-editor pricing with two meters running underneath: media hours AND monthly AI credits. Heavy podcast or video volume burns through the caps fast, and the free tier watermarks 720p exports: model your real production hours before picking a tier. The API changes the arithmetic rather than escaping it. Their own API page states access is included for paying users at no additional cost, but the work it does draws from the same AI credits and media minutes, so automating a pipeline burns the caps faster, not slower. It also stops just short of the finish: the same page says direct media file exports are not supported yet, so the export step stays a manual one in the app. (read on their own API page, 2026-08-14)

video:video.video:title: Devs.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The seat price is the smaller half of the bill. Personal includes $10 of usage a month and Business $21, with model usage metered on top of the seat. The plan cards state the included amount without stating the rate you pay once it runs out, which is exactly the number you need to forecast a real workload. The free plan is a demo rather than a working tier: both builders are limited to "Core", and workflows, APIs and integrations are absent entirely, which is much of what would make the platform useful past a first agent. And for a product sold on IT governance, the governance controls are the ones you cannot buy with a card: SSO, access control lists and white-labelling sit on the Enterprise tier, behind a custom annual contract.

video:video.video:title: Dify Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: 'Free' self-hosting isn't free: you own the servers, updates and reliability, and model usage bills separately once the included message credits run out. Dify Cloud takes that infrastructure work off your hands, but every cloud plan is a single workspace, and multiple workspaces, SSO and a commercial licence sit in quote-only Enterprise. It's powerful, but self-hosting it well needs technical comfort.

video:video.video:title: DigiParser Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Billing is per page, not per document, so multi-page POs and invoices use up the allowance faster than the plan names suggest, and confidence scoring doubles the credits per page. Unused credits expire every month, also on yearly plans, and a charged subscription is not refunded. AI splitting, classification and confidence scores start on Pro at $149 a month billed yearly. The ~99% accuracy, 2,000+ businesses and 5M+ documents on the home page are DigiParser's own figures.

video:video.video:title: Disputifier Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Free to install is doing a lot of work here. All four services bill per event: a fifth of each recovery, $17 to $27.50 an alert, five cents an order twice over, so the cost lands after the fact and scales with exactly the thing you are trying to reduce. Model your worst chargeback month before you switch alerts on, not your average one.
The reviews deserve a straight look too. The 4.6 average across 125 reviews, read again on 17 September 2026, is not a middle: 87% are five stars and twelve of the one hundred and twenty-five are a single star, with almost nothing in between. That shape has held while the count grew: on 22 August the same listing showed 4.6 from 88 reviews with nine one-stars, so both ends have filled at roughly the same rate. The most recent one-star we read, from June 2026, describes a security incident at the vendor and a dispute over unpaid invoices and billing descriptors; Disputifier replied in July that it does not block merchants from moving providers and disputes the account of the charges. We have not verified either side and are not taking one. What the pattern does show is where the friction sits: merchants either rate this perfect or fall out with it over invoices, not over whether disputes were won.
And know what alerts cannot reach. Coverage depends on the shopper's bank and card: smaller issuers do not participate, Amex and Discover frequently cannot be set up, Klarna alerts do not exist yet and PayPal alerts are recent. The prevention rate the vendor quotes is a ceiling for a well-covered card mix, not a promise for yours.

video:video.video:title: DocHub Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free plan's 3 uses a month are shared by editing, self-signing and sign requests, and our test could not show which actions counted. Unlimited sign requests need Pro, whose trial asks for a card and becomes a €16 monthly charge after 30 days unless you cancel.

video:video.video:title: EasyDMARC Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You are buying domains and history, not features, and no longer seats, since every tier now lists unlimited users. Plus covers two domains. Subdomains do not count toward that, the page says they are detected automatically, but a company with a main domain, a second brand and a legacy domain it forgot about is already over. The history window is the part that bites later: three months on Plus means that when you are investigating a spoofing campaign that started in the spring, the reports are gone. And watch the volume ceiling. Read on 4 October 2026, the page's own tooltip says that once you pass your monthly quota, additional reports are not processed until the next billing cycle. There is no overage charge, just a gap in the data, and it opens precisely when a spoofing run inflates your report volume. Size the plan on your busiest month, not your average.

video:video.video:title: Emergent Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The real cost is credit consumption, not the flat sticker -- Emergent's own guide says one prompt can cost from a handful of credits for a small UI tweak to hundreds for a full feature with tests, and a published app keeps drawing credits every month for its hosting tier, so serious builders run through a plan faster than the price list implies. Now do the division, because Emergent's own pricing page doesn't. Standard is $20 for 100 credits, so 20 cents a credit. Pro is $200 for 750, which is 26.7 cents. Moving up a tier makes every unit of work more expensive, not less: Pro costs 33% more per credit than Standard, and annual billing keeps the gap (17 cents against 22.3). That is the opposite of the volume discount the ladder looks like -- you are buying a 1M-token context window, custom agents and priority support, not cheaper work. Above Pro there is no bigger self-serve plan: Business and Enterprise are both quote-only. Top-up packs fill the gap at the Standard rate, 250 credits for $50 or 20 cents a credit, but they are non-refundable. Check what your month actually needs before you upgrade; one Standard month plus purchased extra credits may beat one Pro month. AI-generated code still needs a human eye: review it for security, correctness and maintainability before anything touches real users.

video:video.video:title: Expertise AI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catch is that you can no longer see what this costs. On 3 September 2026 the page still had a ladder: a Free Preview capped at 10 conversations, then Business at $2,000/mo, the $500 Growth tier having been withdrawn in August. By 1 October every amount was gone, the free preview with it, and all three tiers now end in 'Book a demo'. So the price is whatever the call produces, and the only public yardstick is the old $2,000 a month. It's also a RAG agent, so it's only as good as the docs you feed it: give it thin content and it can answer buyers confidently but wrong. Strong for HubSpot-centric B2B teams that are ready to buy through sales; hard to evaluate on your own.

video:video.video:title: FlexiQuiz Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The monthly response caps are the business model: 20 on free, 500 on Essentials, 2,000 on Premium and 25,000 on Enterprise -- one viral quiz or one big exam cohort and you're shopping a tier up. The cap hits the participant, not you: in our test on 20 October 2026 the 21st respondent of the month saw only 'This account has reached the maximum monthly response limit' instead of the quiz. The free plan also stops at 10 questions, a limit that only shows up when you save the eleventh. The per-response price falls steeply as you climb ($0.034, $0.0125, $0.0024 on yearly billing), so the ceiling is the thing to price, not the sticker. Administrator seats are capped separately at 1, 2 and 15, and sharing a login is against the terms.

video:video.video:title: Flippa Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The real cost is the success fee, and it's a flat bracket rate on the whole sale price, not marginal: a mid-five-figure sale can hand over a four- to five-figure commission. Flippa is also a self-serve marketplace: more listings, but more due-diligence burden on you. Verification and quality vary, so buyers must vet hard and sellers should expect tyre-kickers. It's reach and liquidity, not a white-glove broker.

video:video.video:title: Foxit Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Foxit's pitch is being the honest fraction of Acrobat's price, and on the headline numbers it delivers. The catch used to be that e-signing was always a second subscription. As of our 28 August 2026 reading that is only true below Editor+, which now includes Foxit eSign with 150 envelopes a year. The trap has moved rather than gone: buy the $129.99 Editor, then find you need signatures, and Editor plus standalone eSign Essentials is $249.99 a year against $159.99 for the Editor+ that bundles it. AI is still an add-on at $49.99 a year beyond the 300 monthly credits, and in September the FAQ said it is not sold for perpetual licences (the November FAQ no longer says so). Price the basket, not the first line.

video:video.video:title: FreshBooks Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two things multiply the number you first see. The promotional rates end: Lite is $1 a month for the first year and $23 after that, and Plus and Premium are 80% off for three months only. And the meter is billable clients, not invoices or revenue: Lite stops at five, which a freelancer with a handful of retainers passes in their first good quarter, and the step to fifty clients is $43. Then people cost extra on top at $11 each, so a two-person studio on Plus is $54 a month rather than $43. Payroll is a separate $40 plus $6 a head, which is the line most people miss when they compare this against a bookkeeping tool that includes it.

video:video.video:title: Freshservice Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $19 headline rarely survives contact with a real deployment: the ITSM features most IT teams buy for (change/problem management, deeper analytics) live at Pro, and so does Freddy AI Copilot, a $29-an-agent add-on offered only on Pro and Enterprise. Orchestration runs and, from Growth up, 100 asset units come included; you pay extra only past those allowances. Price the tier that contains your must-haves plus the add-ons you would switch on, not the starter row. Within that honesty, it's one of the fastest ITSM tools to actually stand up.

video:video.video:title: Getscreen Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: AnyDesk tends to feel faster and lower-latency, and TeamViewer carries the heavier security/compliance certifications (HIPAA, SOC 2). Getscreen's real edge is that you connect from a browser and that it is cheaper, especially with the lifetime deal; for a one-off session the other person still has to download and run a file.

video:video.video:title: Glide Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Glide meters updates, not just seats. Your bill tracks how busy the app is rather than how many people own a licence. A write-heavy workflow can pass the included 5,000 updates and add 2 cents each without anyone changing plan. The jump from Maker to Business is also steep: $49 to $199 per month on annual billing, and the row ceiling only moves from 25k to 100k. Per Glide's partner team on 18 August 2026, those ceilings track the data source rather than the plan. 25k applies to synced spreadsheet sources whatever you pay, and the 100k+ figures belong to their Big Table source. So an upgrade alone does not lift a spreadsheet-backed app past 25k rows. The pricing page is hard to read for a reason Glide does not dispute. Asked about the Individual and Business tabs, the same team called them audience segmentation. They agreed on 18 August 2026 that the comparison tables confuse, because they never put all plans side by side. And there is a trap before any of that arithmetic applies: everything above describes the classic builder, but the free signup button on glideapps.com does not lead there. We pressed it on 7 September 2026 and landed in GlideOS, the newer AI product, which meters credits instead of updates, starts at $25 a month instead of $199, and describes its free tier only as “limited credits” with no number anywhere in the pricing page or the app. Read the classic prices, click sign up, and you are evaluating something else.

video:video.video:title: Gymcatch Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Card processing fees are charged on top of the subscription and we could not find the rates. There is no free plan or yearly price on the page. We found no dated changelog.

video:video.video:title: Hive Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The seat price is honest bait, the add-on grid is the business model: switch on three add-ons and your $12 seat becomes $27: a la carte flexibility that punishes teams who need the full toolkit. List your must-have modules first and compare the DRESSED price against all-inclusive rivals; for teams needing only core PM, though, Hive is cheap and pleasant. In our test on 21 October 2026 two defaults stood out: onboarding lets everyone on your email domain join the workspace automatically unless you untick it, and completed tasks disappear from the List view behind a filter.

video:video.video:title: Housecall Pro Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The Basic tier is a trap for real field teams: it omits GPS tracking and QuickBooks sync, so most businesses need Essentials or up. And the seats are the expensive part: users beyond the eight on MAX cost $35 a month each, and the page no longer states the extra-seat price on Essentials, on top of card processing quoted as 'as low as' 2.59% and a 1% fee on bank payments. Price the tier and the headcount you'll actually need.

video:video.video:title: Hubstaff Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The seat definition is the whole story and they state it plainly, which deserves credit: you pay for every seat you have created, not every person actually being tracked. So an account that grew with your headcount and never got tidied up is billing you for people who left. Audit your seat list before renewal, not after. The second thing is that features on the lower tiers are add-ons rather than inclusions: Insights, Tasks, Silent app and extra screenshots at $2.50 a seat a month, Locations at $3.33, so the plan you priced and the plan that does what you watched in the demo may differ by ten dollars a seat. And be clear with yourself about why you are buying it: screenshots and activity levels change how a team feels about their work, and that cost does not appear on any pricing page.

video:video.video:title: Imagify Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: A prepaid yearly plan is not refunded. The free tier's 20MB a month and 2MB per image are only enough for a test, Growth charges $5 for each extra GB, and Infinite's unlimited use falls under a fair-use clause. In our test on 21 October 2026 the free quota counted the original file size, not the compressed result (a 11.8KB and a 48.9KB image moved the counter to 61.44KB), a 3.4MB file was refused at the 2MB cap without using quota, and the 'You saved' total on the web app's optimizer page showed the size after compression instead of the saving; the History page had the right figures.

video:video.video:title: InVideo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catch is the credit model: each plan is a fixed monthly credit allowance that different models consume at different rates, and unused credits do not roll over, so a heavy month can exhaust an allowance long before it renews while a slow month simply wastes what you paid for. The pricing page lists no free tier, but on 22 November 2026 a new account opened on a Free plan with 50 credits; in our test one prompt used 26.4 of them and the voiceover still needed a paid plan. AI video is fast but generic by default: templated output needs real editing and brand direction to not look like everyone else's. Treat it as a first-draft engine, not a finished-studio replacement.

video:video.video:title: Jibble Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Free forever with unlimited users holds up: the plan a new account lands on is Free, €0, with no card. What free leaves out is now readable too, because Jibble's own plan comparison sits inside the app even though the public pricing page is gone. The biggest gaps for a payroll process are timesheet approvals, automatic break deductions and more than one admin; our hands-on test below lists everything Free leaves out and keeps.
Two things to know before you build a process on it. A new organisation starts with a 14-day trial of the paid features, so for the first two weeks nothing looks locked; the limits above only show from day 15. Set up your workflow on what Free keeps, not on what week one showed you. And the paid tiers are cheap per head but add up: timesheet approvals and groups start at €1.79 per user a month on annual billing, €2.99 if you pay monthly, so a team of 25 pays €537 a year for the step most payroll processes need first.

video:video.video:title: Leavo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The tidy per-user numbers are annual-billed, and it's priced per seat: every employee you track adds to the bill, with no volume break published (large teams are told to ask sales). And the “free” is a 30-day trial, not a permanent free tier: budget for the paid plan from day 31.

video:video.video:title: Lindy.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Cost tracks headcount as well as output: every colleague who so much as @mentions Lindy in Slack takes a seat, and a seat you remove runs to the end of the cycle with no mid-cycle proration. Credits are sized in ranges (an everyday ask is 2-250, a big build 1,000-2,500), so a month is still an estimate. And the entry price itself was served in two versions on 8 November 2026: $29.99 for 3,000 credits or $49.99 for 5,000.

video:video.video:title: Lovable Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You do not know what a change costs until it is done. Lovable prices each build message by the work it turns out to involve, from about half a credit for a styling tweak to two credits for a page with images, so a credit budget is an estimate, not a price list. The second catch is easy to miss: the app you publish runs its database, hosting and AI features on a separate monthly Cloud grant of 20 credits. Lovable's own documentation says a published app stays live when those credits run out, but its backend services and AI features pause, so an app that works on day one can stop saving data later in the month. The larger Pro tiers are no cheaper per credit until 1,200 credits a month, so buying ahead saves nothing below that.

video:video.video:title: Mera Work Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The price is low and the feature list is long; the catch sits in the data rather than the bill. Mera Work keeps your records for 90 days. The pricing table says data retention up to three months, and the privacy policy spells it out: unless your order form says otherwise, customer data is held on a rolling 90-day basis and anything older may be deleted automatically from production. That rules it out as the place you look back from over a year: an annual review, a client disputing hours billed last spring, a payroll audit. Export the timesheets and attendance you need every month, or get a longer retention period written into the order form before you roll it out.
This is monitoring software, not only a timer. The feature table lists screenshots, live screen streaming, keyboard and mouse activity tracking and a stealth mode. Mera Work's own pages are more careful than the word keystroke suggests: its keystroke feature records how much typing happened and when, not the keys or words themselves, and screenshots can be blurred and limited by role. But whether you may run screenshots, live view or a hidden agent on your staff's computers is a question for your employment adviser, not the vendor, and data-protection rules in Europe generally expect employees to be told what is recorded. Decide the policy first and tell people what the agent captures.
Two practical points. The company behind it, Aapna Infotheek Private Limited, is based in New Delhi, and its privacy policy says data may be hosted or processed in India. The hosting page, read 25 November 2026, says the standard cloud runs on Microsoft Azure in India, the UAE, Australia and the United States, with private cloud and on premise reserved for enterprise customers; if location matters, ask which region your account lands in and put it in the contract. And the review sites we normally read, Capterra and G2, blocked our reader on 30 September 2026. The one we could read, SoftwareSuggest, shows six reviews from 2

video:video.video:title: MigrationPro Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Start with the listing, because it went away and came back. On 5 October 2026 the Shopify App Store listing said the app was not currently available, with no install button and no review page; on 17 November 2026 it was live again with an Install button and 190 reviews, and the app installed normally in our own test. The vendor has not said why the listing was unavailable.
The listing tells you nothing about what this costs: “Free to install. Additional charges may apply”, and a single plan block saying pricing is tailored to the entities you migrate. The number lives on the vendor's calculator, and the first number you find there, $29, is the floor for the smallest store on the self-service route, not the price for yours. Their own homepage says a typical store lands between $49 and $299. Run the calculator before you form an opinion about value.
The add-on structure used to be the unknowable part, and as of 18 September 2026 it is not: the pricing page lists every add-on with a price, from $19 to $39, and marks all of them included on the managed plan. That is a real improvement in what a buyer can read before committing. It also makes the self-service route look less like $29: the 301 redirects add-on, which is the one thing a migrating store can least afford to get wrong, is a $29 extra on a $29 migration.
The marketing still runs ahead of the evidence. The pricing page says “Trusted by 250,000+ stores”, the homepage uses the same figure for migrations, and the FAQ says 250,000+ migrations over 13 years: one number doing three different jobs. The same page, and an FAQ answer saying the app is available on the Shopify App Store, still claim 5.0 from 170+ verified reviews, against a listing that showed 186 on 18 September, of which 181 were five star, 4 four star and one a single star, and 190 on 17 November 2026. Those reviews were good; weigh them rather than the banner.
One practical limit sits in the reviews rather than the marketing. The FAQ says most sto

video:video.video:title: MindStudio Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The no-markup model pass-through is fair, but it also means your real cost is subscription PLUS model spend, and an agent that loops or processes big documents burns provider credits invisibly until you set limits. The honest build discipline: start every agent with usage caps, and treat 'no-code' as no-code for the plumbing: the logic design and prompt quality are still entirely on you.

video:video.video:title: Miro Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Per-member pricing charges for every member added to the workspace, so an org-wide rollout multiplies at full headcount, and the free plan's cap of 3 editable boards is workspace-wide, not per person. In our test on 20 October 2026 Miro did not block a fourth board: it warned that the oldest board would become view-only, and a new free team already starts with one board made for you. Model who needs to edit before you buy seats.

video:video.video:title: Modge Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The numbers on Modge's own pages do not agree with each other. The homepage says trusted by 1,000+ teams, the affiliate page says 1,800+ teams, the pricing page says over 2,000 users; the pricing page also shows three star ratings, 4.6 from 1,500 reviews, 4.8 from 2,000 and 4.2 from 800, without naming a single platform they come from. None of that touches the product, but it is the kind of copy a buyer should not repeat in a business case. What does touch the product is the comparison table: SSO through SAML 2.0, SOC 2 Type II and ISO 9001 are all marked soon, and HIPAA compliant appears with no report behind it. If your security review needs a document today, there is none to hand over. The desktop agent is macOS and Windows only, and the pricing page mentions no mobile app or GPS, so field teams are out of scope.

video:video.video:title: Murf Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is generation hours per YEAR, not per month: 24 hours sounds generous until you count retakes, because every text edit regenerates the whole sub-block and bills again. Replaying is free, and in our test on 20 October 2026 the on-screen meter only caught up after a page reload. Voice quality is strong, but the honest test for any TTS is your specific language, names and jargon: generate your hardest paragraph in the trial before subscribing, because demo voices always sound better than your edge cases.

video:video.video:title: Navan Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: 'Free' is real but has a mechanism: Navan earns commission on bookings made through its inventory, so the platform's incentive is that your travel flows through Navan, and pricing on specific routes/hotels deserves an occasional spot-check against direct booking. The free Business plan stops at 300 employees and lists corporate negotiated rates as an Enterprise feature; expense management is free for 5 users and $15 per user per month after that.

video:video.video:title: Ngram Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The sticker price buys a credit allowance, not finished video, and the two are easy to confuse. Premium AI generation runs from 10 credits a second, so Basic's 3,000 credits a month come out at roughly 300 seconds: about five minutes of generated footage. Ngram says as much on the page: generation seconds measure premium AI-generated footage, not final video length, and manual editing and exports are unlimited on paid plans. So the tier you need tracks how much AI footage you generate, not how many videos you publish.
The top-up economics run the wrong way for small buyers. Extra credits cost 1,000 for $40 on Free, $20 on Basic, $15 on Premium and $10 on Ultimate: the cheapest plan pays four times per credit what the dearest one pays. Anyone topping up regularly on Basic is paying a premium for staying on the cheap tier, and should price the next tier against a month of actual top-ups rather than against the headline gap between the two.
Two smaller things before you pick. Export quality is tiered (720p on Basic, 1080p on Premium, 4K on Ultimate) so the resolution you need may set your plan before the credits do. And image and audio generation still consume credits on Basic, going unlimited only from Premium up.

video:video.video:title: Nouswise Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Their own site does not agree with itself about what this costs, and we have now checked that twice. The pricing page says Essential 19.99$/month and Pro 49.99$/month; the homepage, read the same day, shows a pricing block with $10.00 and $40.00. We put the gap to Nouswise, and on 18 Aug 2026 their partner manager answered that the homepage figures are a counter animation and that a normal browser with JavaScript enabled would show 19.99 and 49.99. We did exactly that check the same day (an ordinary browser, JavaScript on, waiting for the animation to settle) and the homepage still read $10.00 for Essential and $40.00 for Professional. So the gap is real, the vendor's own explanation for it did not hold, and neither page flags the other. Get the number in writing for the tier and the billing period you want before you put a card in, because there is a documented chance of paying double what a landing page just promised you.
The headline claim needs the same care. The homepage says “100% Verifiable AI Answers” and that answers are “solely drawn from the provided sources, reducing any fact fabrication to zero”. That is Nouswise describing Nouswise: nobody independent has tested it and neither have we. Grounding an answer in a curated library does cut invention, but it does not make retrieval, ranking or summarising error-free, and it cannot make an answer better than the library it came from. If your library is thin, outdated or one-sided, a confident grounded answer is still the wrong answer: with a citation attached. Two other numbers on that page, the 25% of the workweek spent searching and the 2.4 billion hours a year inside the Fortune 500, carry no source on the page at all.
Three smaller things worth knowing. The source ceilings are low for organisational use (100 sources on Starter, 300 on Essential) and unlimited sources only start at Pro. The per-day limits on reports, flashcards and quizzes carry an asterisk explained only as “Limits are accumulative”, wh

video:video.video:title: Pangram Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The unavoidable honest limit of every AI detector, including accurate ones: it is never infallible. It will occasionally flag human writing as AI (false positives) and miss some AI text, so it must be used as a signal, never as sole proof for high-stakes calls like academic penalties or hiring. Pangram's pitch is fewer false positives than rivals, which is real progress, but 'fewer' is not 'none'. Pair it with human judgment and the credit meter with your actual volume: the free tier's 2,000 words a day are 20 credits rounded up per check, which in our test meant ten checks of 150 words rather than twenty.

video:video.video:title: Passpack Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The honest trade-off is maturity, not security. The interface is plain, the mobile side is very new, and some users report slow support and billing hiccups. You are trading polish and a settled mobile experience for price and solid zero-knowledge encryption.
Android is the concrete form of that trade. The iOS app arrived on 10 August 2026; twenty-seven days later, on 6 September 2026, there was still no Android app. Passpack's own Downloads menu offered only iOS and the browser extension, and a Google Play search for 'passpack' that day returned thirteen apps, all of them rival password managers and none of them this one. By 17 November 2026 the Downloads menu linked an Android app on Google Play (Passpack, Inc.; last updated 16 October 2026, 10+ downloads). It exists now, but it is the newest and least tested part of the product.
Their own pages lag their announcements, too, though less than they did. Passpack told partners on 2 September 2026 that TOTP now works on every plan, and on 3 September the word appeared on neither the plans nor the key-features page; by 6 September the plans comparison table lists both TOTP and 'Mobile app for iOS', in the section that carries no plan exclusions. The key-features page has not caught up: on 6 September it still listed 'Mobile & Browser Extensions' under New Features Coming Soon, four weeks after iOS shipped and with the extensions already sold on the plans page. Read the plans table rather than the newsletter, and confirm stored TOTP codes inside the 28-day trial.

video:video.video:title: Pdfdodo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The refund rules contradict each other: the FAQ says no refunds of any kind, the terms promise refunds within 30 days of purchase. The yearly Solo card has been repriced since our first reading, from $20 a month beside $200 billed yearly (16 October) to $20.83 a month and $250 billed yearly (6 November), so check the amount at checkout, and no plan names its currency. Cancelling means sending an email rather than a button in the app.

video:video.video:title: QuickBooks UK Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The 90% offer is the number to be careful with, because it is the one you will see everywhere and it is not what you will pay. On monthly billing the page says six months: Sole Trader Plus shows £1 and renews at £10 a month, Plus shows £6 and renews at £60 (list prices read 27 November 2026). That tenfold step arrives in month seven, on a tool you will by then have your entire bookkeeping inside, which is precisely when switching is hardest. Add 20% VAT on top of every figure, and add payroll separately if you need it. Budget from the list price and treat the discount as a half-year rebate, not as the price.

video:video.video:title: QuillBot Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free tier is deliberately narrow: 125 words per paraphrase and two of the modes. The honest framing is that this is a box of writing utilities -- paraphraser, grammar, plagiarism, AI detection -- rather than somewhere you actually write. General AI chat tools now overlap much of it. And treat the free AI detector as weak: in our test of 1 October 2026 it rated four plainly written machine texts 100% human and only caught a paragraph full of stock chatbot phrases. Note the sticker too: the advertised €8.33 a month assumes you pay for the year, and month-to-month is €19.95, about 2.4 times as much.

video:video.video:title: Reclaim.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The magic only works on a calendar it can write to. Google Calendar was first, but Microsoft 365, Outlook.com and Exchange-backed accounts are supported too (reclaim.ai/integrations/outlook-calendar, read 15 September 2026); Reclaim's own help centre still lists hosted and on-premise Exchange as unsupported. The free tier is quite limited. A genuine time-saver for the right setup, useless for the wrong one.

video:video.video:title: Recruit CRM Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The headline seat price is not the whole bill: the features recruiters use daily for outreach run on credits, and LinkedIn messaging alone uses 150 credits per user a month while Pro includes 100. The pricing table says unlimited candidates and contacts, but the help centre sets per-user record limits (10,000 each on Pro). Annual billing is charged upfront and the subscription article rules out refunds for unused time, so a wrong tier choice is expensive to undo.

video:video.video:title: Replit Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The subscription price is fixed; the paid Agent work is not. Everyday building can run in Free Mode at no extra cost, within an allowance that resets every five hours on Core and Pro and a daily cap on Starter, but anything past it is billed by effort, and only Pro's unused credits roll over, for two months. Replit asks before each paid request starts and lets you set a budget, so set one before long sessions. Great for learning and prototyping; watch the meter for production work.

video:video.video:title: SMTP2GO Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's the pragmatic middle of email infrastructure: simpler and better-supported than the hyperscale APIs, cheaper than most, with useful reporting, but sending reputation is still yours to earn. A relay delivers what your domain deserves: without proper SPF/DKIM/DMARC and list hygiene, no provider saves you. Check the overage rate for your tier before you size up: on the 10,000 plan an extra thousand emails costs $1.20 against the $1.50 a thousand you already pay, and the 50,000 plan at $30 works out cheaper per email than Professional at $75.

video:video.video:title: ServiceM8 Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Unlimited users on every paid tier is unusual in this category and worth saying first: put your whole crew in without the bill moving. The meter is jobs instead, and jobs are the thing you least control. Fifty a month on Starter is roughly two a working day, which a two-van operation passes in a busy month, and the next step is not a small one, it is $29 to $79. Count your jobs in your best month rather than your average, because that is the month that will bump you, and a seasonal trade will spend part of the year paying for a tier it does not need. The free tier at 30 jobs and one user is a real trial, not a plan.

video:video.video:title: Shiftie Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's focused, affordable rota software, which means it does scheduling, clock-ins, leave and swaps well, but it isn't a full HR or payroll platform, so a growing business will still bolt on payroll and HR tools around it. Pricing is low, but the per-active-employee model means a large seasonal team in a busy month costs more than the headline suggests. For shift-based scheduling specifically, it's a clean, cheap fit.

video:video.video:title: Shippo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing is honest but layered. The free tier stops at 30 labels a month, and its 5¢ per label on your own carrier accounts quietly adds up. Pro looks like a flat $17 a month until you read the comparison table: it covers up to 10,000 shipments and then bills $0.08 for every label beyond that, so a good sales month adds a variable line to a subscription that reads as fixed. Address validation outside the US is metered too, at 9¢, 8¢ or 6¢ depending on plan. The real money is elsewhere anyway: in the carrier rate discounts, which vary by lane and weight. Run your five most common shipments through it against your current rates; that comparison decides, not the subscription price.

video:video.video:title: Shore Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's built for local appointment businesses in the German-speaking market, and the package split shows it: booking and the till are sold as separate lines, and only All-in-One carries both. Card fees are quoted on your sales rather than published, so the package price is not the whole bill - and the POS is only sold in Germany, Austria and Switzerland.

video:video.video:title: ShortlistIQ Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: No yearly prices are shown although the FAQ mentions yearly plans, and the cards do not name their currency. Basic covers only 20 applicants a month with a single AI assistant. Unused or partly used service is not refunded on early cancellation, and the homepage selling point, that candidates cannot tell the AI from a person, puts the duty to disclose on you.

video:video.video:title: Signable Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Business and Enterprise prices are only 'from' figures and go through sales, and the overage fee for envelopes beyond your allowance is not published. Unused envelopes on a paid plan are lost at the end of the billing period. The API, bulk send and Qualified Electronic Signatures all start on Business, from £100 a month, not on Essentials.

video:video.video:title: SimplyBook.me Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The plan ladder is set by bookings per month and by how many custom features you may switch on, and those two ceilings move independently, so you can outgrow a plan on features while nowhere near the booking cap, or the reverse. Free and Basic also carry SimplyBook.me branding on your booking page; white-label starts at Premium. Two integration limits sit in their own documentation. Calendar Sync works with web calendars only, and the help page warns it may not work with Microsoft Exchange calendars. The Zapier connector, which gained a create-booking action in June 2026, stops working once HIPAA or Google Authenticator is switched on, so the practices most likely to need HIPAA lose the Zapier route.

video:video.video:title: SmartSuite Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's a broad, do-everything work-management platform, so the power comes with a learning curve and a per-seat cost that adds up for bigger teams: a single source of truth if you commit, overkill if you just need a task list. One gate comes before all of that: on 21 October 2026 the trial sign-up refused both addresses we tried, each on our own company domain, with 'Please use your business email.' We could not get in, so this review still describes SmartSuite from its own pages, not from use.

video:video.video:title: Softr Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Builder seats are billed on top of the plan, and pricing counts builders and app users separately, so a public-facing app with a lot of end users gets expensive fast. Watch the overage rate as well as the plan: extra app users are $1 a month on Pro but $2 on Business, so the dearer plan meters growth at double the rate. It fits internal tools and client portals with a known audience, not an open signup. In our test on 21 October 2026 a new account started on a 7-day Business trial that drops back to Free on its own, and two articles we added did not appear in the template's 'Latest articles' list, although they did appear in their collection and in search.

video:video.video:title: Sunsama Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: There is no free plan after the 14-day trial and no cheaper tier: Pro at $22 a month billed monthly, or $17 billed yearly, per person, is the only self-serve option. Until at least 19 September 2026 the pricing page also contradicted itself (its FAQ said $25 and $20); by 19 November the FAQ matched the plan card. The other thing to be clear about is that this is per person with no team discount mentioned: two people is two subscriptions, and their own example says $44 a month.

video:video.video:title: SurveyMonkey Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free tier is a teaser. Response caps on the self-serve plans trigger $0.15-per-response overages (US rate; Enterprise contracts set their own limits) that become a hidden cost on big studies. Branding and customisation are limited, and a lot of the good analytics and logic sit behind higher tiers.

video:video.video:title: Survicate Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The plan is metered by response volume, not by surveys: a viral NPS month can push you a tier up, and the free plan's 30-day retention quietly deletes your history. Mind the billing asymmetry too: Starter is monthly-only while Growth and up expect an annual commitment.

video:video.video:title: Synthesia Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The minute caps are tight: Starter's 1,250 credits a month is roughly 10 to 12 minutes of finished video, and the meter counts seconds. A small edit generated again cost us 4 credits rather than the whole video, but the free plan put that second render in a 15-minute queue. Fantastic for avatar-led training and explainers without a studio, but not for high-volume or cinematic production. And check the plan at checkout: the app and the public pricing page described different plans on the same day (1 October 2026), and the page is priced differently in dollars and euros.

video:video.video:title: Team Pulse Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The tiers gate on TWO axes at once (member count and project/pipeline count) so you can hit a wall on either. The CRM pipeline is a big part of the pitch, but it doesn't exist below the $79 Growth plan (Free and Starter have none), and member limits are tight: Starter is a single seat, Growth just three. The headline rates are the annual ones; month-to-month costs 25 to 34% more ($39 against $29 on Starter, $99 against $79 on Growth).

video:video.video:title: Tellent Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Tellent's modular shape is useful (you can buy just the ATS, or just the HRIS) but nothing is priced in public: every tier on tellent.com/pricing ends in 'Get a demo' (read in a browser on 9 September 2026), and recruitee.com/pricing carries no figures either. Ask for Start, Advance and Optimize quoted together with their renewal prices, because you have no anchor to check a single number against. And as with every ATS, workflow fit (approval chains, careers-site needs, integrations with your assessment tools) matters more than the feature list; the free trial is enough to run one real vacancy through, so do that.

video:video.video:title: TestGorilla Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The Assessments bill is set by credits, and the page does not say how many credits its 'from' prices include. Core starts from $77 a month billed annually or from $287 billed monthly; that gap is far wider than the 25% annual saving the page advertises, so the two floors are different allowances. An AI interview costs 2 credits a candidate and a skills test 1, so the real price depends on how you build each assessment and how many people you invite. Get the credit allowance in writing before you compare it with a per-seat tool.

video:video.video:title: TextExpander Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: On a Mac the operating system already does the basic job free: Apple's built-in Text Replacement syncs static snippets across your Apple devices, though Apple's own documentation notes it is not available in every app. And Espanso covers the power-user case free and open source on Mac, Windows and Linux. On Windows there is no built-in equivalent (contrary to a widely repeated claim, PowerToys has no text-expansion utility), so the case for paying is stronger there. On mobile, only iPhone and iPad are covered: the vendor's mobile page, read 9 October 2026, offers a keyboard app for those, while Android is still a beta signup. Then add the snippet activity history: nothing at all on the free plan, only 24 hours on the $5 Pro tier, 7 days on Business, and unlimited only on Enterprise. Add the vendor's own note that buyers in VAT/GST countries including the EU, UK and Australia may see an estimated 20% uplift on the listed USD price (read 21 July 2026). For one person with a few dozen fixed snippets, the honest answer is usually don't.

video:video.video:title: Todoist Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free plan's 5-project cap, and reminders that fire only at the moment a task comes due, push most serious users to Pro quickly, but Pro is cheap. In our test on 20 October 2026 the sixth project was not created: the attempt opened a 7-day Pro trial offer instead. It's a personal/team task manager, not a full project platform, so don't expect Gantt-level PM.

video:video.video:title: Top Echelon Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Almost everything people shop for sits in Professional, not Standard: Smart-TE AI, automations, sequences, inbound email sync and API access are all one tier up, so Standard is a competent but plain ATS. The bigger thing to price honestly is that TE Recruit and TE Network are two separate subscriptions. The network is billed per agency on top of your seats, so "Top Echelon" can mean two bills. And taking the network month-to-month adds a $350 one-time startup fee that annual billing waives.

video:video.video:title: Tresorit Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You pay the Swiss-E2EE premium (noticeably above mainstream clouds and above Proton Drive per GB) and the encryption trade-offs are inherent: no server-side content search, more deliberate sharing flows, and credential/recovery discipline is on you. For regulated teams that's exactly the deal; for casual storage it's over-engineering.

video:video.video:title: Unleashed Software Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The 100 sales orders a month included on both bundles is the number that decides your bill, not the $399. A wholesaler running 1,500 orders with six users who wants phone support pays $399 for Core, $200 for the order tier, $207 for three extra seats and $99 for Standard support. That is $905 a month, or 2.3 times the headline, before a one-off onboarding fee of at least $449. Support being a paid add-on rather than part of the plan is the detail most comparison tables miss. Price the bundle you will actually be on: count your busiest month's orders, your real seat count, and decide whether you can live without phone support, then compare that total against the alternatives rather than comparing entry prices.

video:video.video:title: UserHelp.co Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: No refund rule, seat count, recording retention or length of one-time access is stated on the pricing page or in the terms, which date from April 2024. Basic is limited to one project and shows a watermark, and the card does not name its currency. In our test on 18 November 2026 the free plan showed only the 5 oldest responses.

video:video.video:title: WPForms Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The prices on the pricing page are introductory: every plan renews at double the displayed price, and no end date for the introductory offer is given. A licence covers a fixed number of sites (1, 3, 5 or unlimited). Payment add-ons sit on the higher plans, and the free version or an inactive licence adds a 3% platform fee on payments.

video:video.video:title: World Businesses for Sale Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: On the broker plans you pay twice: a listing fee up front AND commission when it sells (3% on Basic, 2% on Standard, 1% on Premium) on contracts of 6, 9 and 12 months. Only Premium stays live until sold with free renewals, so on the lower tiers a business that has not sold needs a paid renewal, and for a slow sale £999 once costs about the same as £499 twice. Every tier says commission is payable only when they introduce the buyer, which is exactly the clause to read in the contract before you sign. If you want no commission at all, the pay-as-you-go plans start at £49 a month, or £147 for six months: far cheaper up front, but those are listings, not broker introductions. As with any marketplace, the fee buys exposure, not a guaranteed sale.

video:video.video:title: eBillity Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Workforce and Premium add a base fee on top of the per-user price, which weighs heavily on small teams. Fees are paid in advance and are non-refundable, with no refunds for downgrades or unused months, and seats you remove from an annual plan stay paid until renewal. There is no free plan, and the help articles still describe older product names and plans.

video:video.video:title: xTiles Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free plan keeps only the current and the previous week of planner history open (the pricing page says two weeks; in our test on 21 October 2026 everything older was greyed out behind Plus) and caps uploads at 5MB, so anyone using it as a daily planner will need Plus. Pro's headline is AI control of your workspace, but several of its AI permissions, including editing structure and access rights, are still marked soon. Refund windows are short on monthly plans, 72 hours, and discounted plans are not refundable at all. Only annual Plus can be upgraded to Pro with a credit for what you paid. Prices are per user and VAT may apply. The user count on the site is xTiles' own claim. Our team tested the free plan on 21 October 2026; the findings are further down this page.
